title: Spotting 'true but does not explain' distractors
blurb: Recognize the examiner's favourite trap: a correct statement from the manual that does not explain the situation.
question: An option says 'Yes, because highlight reports are a time-driven control.' That is true. So why is it wrong?

teach.h: True is not the same as right
teach.body: The most common Practitioner distractor is a statement that is accurate in the manual but does not explain why the action in the question is appropriate or not. The official rationales often reject such options with words to the effect of 'this is true, but it does not explain why...'. Your job is not to find a true statement; it is to find the reason that accounts for this particular situation.

steps.label: Ask: does it explain?
steps.sub: Would this reason justify THIS action?

steps.label: Find the link
steps.sub: It should tie to a fact in the stem

head: Shape
Example on progress
rows: Board sets stage tolerances (when the issue is a WP)
A fact about a different activity
Exception plans are prepared in SB
Stages give the board decision points
teach.caption: Each statement is true. None explains why a project manager handled a delay inside tolerance.

teach.h: Manage by exception in one paragraph
teach.body: Each management level delegates authority to the next with tolerances across the seven aspects of performance: benefits, cost, time, quality, scope, sustainability and risk. While work is forecast to stay within tolerance, the lower level gets on with it. When a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, that is an exception and it goes up a level as early as possible. Decisions are made at the most local level where the knowledge sits.

Brennan Mutual (scenario S6) is migrating applications to the cloud. In wave 2, a firewall fault puts eight applications ten days behind. The board's stage time tolerance is three weeks. Project manager Mairi Campbell moves the affected applications to a later slot in the same stage, recovers the time and reports it in her next highlight report. How well does this apply 'manage by exception'? Well: the deviation is within stage tolerance, so the project manager deals with it.

rows.label: A
values: Well: within stage tolerance, the PM acts

rows.label: C
values: Poorly: every delay goes to the board

rows.label: D
values: Poorly: the board sets stage tolerances

teach.caption: B and D are both true statements. Neither explains whether handling the delay herself was right.

teach.h: Where does a forecast deviation go?

children.label: TM raises an issue to the PM

teach.caption: Within stage tolerance the project manager takes corrective action in controlling a stage; no exception report is needed.

teach.text: An issue that the project manager can resolve within stage tolerance needs no exception report: it is handled in controlling a stage, with an issue report if formal. And an exception is a FORECAST breach: you do not wait for the tolerance to be broken before escalating.

items: Most wrong reasons are true statements that do not explain the situation.
Use the 'because' test: does this reason justify THIS action?
Tolerances: business layer sets project, board sets stage, PM sets work package.
Within tolerance the level below acts; a forecast breach is escalated early.
Data and systems support forecasts; management levels set tolerances.

summary: You can now spot options that state a true fact from the manual without explaining the situation, and reject them with the 'because' test. You can also judge how well the S6 project applies manage by exception and the progress practice.

A.q: On Brennan Mutual's Project Skyline, a Stratoshift team in Pune forecasts that its migration work package will finish three days late. The work package time tolerance set by the project manager is one week. The team manager records the forecast in the next checkpoint report. How well does this apply the 'manage by exception' principle, and why?
options: Well, because the forecast stays within the work package tolerance
Well, because checkpoint reports follow the work package frequency
Poorly, because any forecast delay should be raised with the board
Poorly, because the PM should set tolerances for each team member
A.why: Within work package tolerance the team manager carries on and reports normally; only a forecast breach would go to the project manager as an issue (2.5, 11.2.1).

whyNot.1: True that checkpoint frequency is set in the work package, but that does not explain why no escalation is needed.
whyNot.2: Deviations within tolerance are handled at the level that holds the tolerance.
whyNot.3: Team managers set tolerances for team members; the PM sets work package tolerances.

A.q: At the first board meeting for Project Skyline, the project board agrees a project cost tolerance of plus or minus 7.5% and records it in the PID, without referring it to the society's executive committee, which commissioned the project. Is this an appropriate application of the 'progress' practice, and why?
options: Yes, because the board sets tolerances for the aspects of performance
Yes, because cost is one of the seven aspects that tolerances cover
No, because project-level tolerances are set by the business layer
No, because cost tolerance is held in each work package description
A.why: The business layer sets project tolerances; the board sets stage tolerances within them (11.2.1).

whyNot.0: The board sets stage tolerances, not project tolerances, so this reason is wrong for this action.
whyNot.1: True that cost is a tolerance area, but this does not explain who should set the project tolerance.
whyNot.3: Work package tolerances are set by the PM; the question concerns the project level.

A.q: For Project Skyline, the board agrees with the project manager that highlight reports will be fortnightly during the three wave migrations and monthly during decommissioning, as the waves carry most risk to member services. Is this an appropriate application of the 'progress' practice, and why?
options: Yes, because highlight reports are a time-driven control
Yes, because report frequency should match the control needed
No, because the reporting frequency is fixed for the project
No, because highlight reports are produced at stage ends
A.why: Reporting frequency should reflect the level of control required, so riskier periods justify more frequent reports (11.2.4).

whyNot.0: True that highlight reports are time-driven, but this does not explain varying their frequency.
whyNot.2: Frequency is set for the control needed and can differ between stages.
whyNot.3: Highlight reports are periodic within a stage; end stage reports come at stage ends.

B.q: During Project Skyline's wave 1, a firewall fault delays two applications by four days. The stage time tolerance is two weeks and the project manager can recover the delay within the stage. She raises an exception report to the board. Is this an appropriate application of the 'progress' practice, and why?
options: Yes, because the board should be alerted early to any deviation
Yes, because exception reports are an event-driven control
No, because the team manager should report it to the board directly
No, because a delay within stage tolerance is the PM's to handle
B.why: Only forecast breaches of stage or project tolerance go to the board; within tolerance the PM takes corrective action and no exception report is needed (11.2.6).

whyNot.0: Early alerts apply to forecast breaches of tolerance, which this is not.
whyNot.1: True that exception reports are event-driven, but this does not explain raising one here.
whyNot.2: Team managers report to the project manager, not the board.

B.q: At the end of Project Skyline's foundations stage, the project manager produces an end stage report so the board can decide whether to authorize the wave migration stage. What type of control is this, and why?
options: Event-driven, as it is triggered by reaching the end of a stage
Time-driven, as each stage has a planned duration in the plan
Event-driven, as it is triggered by a breach of stage tolerance
Time-driven, as it is produced at intervals set by the board
B.why: Controls triggered by a specific event, such as the end of a stage, are event-driven (11.2.2).

whyNot.1: Stages have planned durations, but the report is triggered by the stage ending, an event.
whyNot.2: Right type, wrong trigger: a tolerance breach triggers an exception report, not an end stage report.
whyNot.3: Reports at board-set intervals are highlight reports, which are time-driven.

B.q: Project Skyline's project manager proposes that the new progress dashboard should calculate each migration wave's time tolerance from the durations of earlier waves, replacing tolerances agreed with the board. Is this an appropriate application of the 'progress' practice, and why?
options: Yes, because past performance data helps predict future performance
Yes, because automation removes the manual merging of data sources
No, because forecasting is not part of the progress practice
No, because tolerances are set by management levels, not by systems
B.why: Data and systems support tracking and forecasting, but tolerances are set by the management levels (11.2.7, 11.2.1).

whyNot.0: True that past data aids forecasting, but this does not justify a system setting tolerances.
whyNot.1: True that automation reduces manual consolidation, but it does not explain who sets tolerances.
whyNot.2: Forecasting is part of the progress practice (11.2.5).

C.q: On Project Skyline, wave 3 has not slipped yet, but the Pune team now forecasts that the final wave will miss the stage end date by five weeks. The stage time tolerance is three weeks. The project manager decides to wait until the delay has actually happened before telling the board. How well does this apply the 'manage by exception' principle, and why?
options: Well, because the PM has authority to manage the stage day to day
Well, because escalation is needed once a breach has actually occurred
Poorly, because a forecast stage tolerance breach should be escalated
Poorly, because the team manager should report directly to the board
C.why: An exception is a forecast breach of tolerance, and the next level should be alerted as early as possible (2.5, 11.3.1).

whyNot.0: True that the PM manages day to day, but that authority ends where stage tolerance is forecast to be exceeded.
whyNot.1: Exceptions are forecasts; waiting for the actual breach removes the board's chance to act early.
whyNot.3: Team managers escalate to the project manager, who escalates to the board.

C.q: Skyline's project manager sends the board an exception report showing the stage cost forecast to exceed its tolerance, with options and a recommendation. The board decides to ask her for an exception plan. Is this an appropriate application of the 'progress' practice, and why?
options: Yes, because the board decides on breaches of stage tolerance
Yes, because exception plans are prepared in controlling a stage
No, because stage tolerance breaches are for the business layer
No, because the PM should prepare the plan before reporting
C.why: The board decides on forecast breaches of stage tolerance and may request an exception plan, which the PM prepares in managing a stage boundary (11.3.1).

whyNot.1: Exception plans are prepared in managing a stage boundary, so this reason is wrong.
whyNot.2: The business layer decides on project tolerance breaches; stage breaches go to the board.
whyNot.3: The board first decides what to do; an exception plan follows its request.

C.q: A delay by Brennan Mutual's core banking vendor means Project Skyline's end date is now forecast to exceed the project time tolerance set by the society's executive committee. The project board approves an exception plan itself, without referring the matter to the executive committee. Is this an appropriate application of the 'manage by exception' principle, and why?
options: Yes, because the board approves exception plans in directing a project
Yes, because the executive is accountable for the project's success
No, because the business layer prepares exception plans at project level
No, because a forecast project tolerance breach is for the business layer
C.why: The business layer sets project tolerances and decides on forecast breaches of them; the board decides on stage tolerance breaches (11.2.1, 11.3.1).

whyNot.0: True that the board approves stage-level exception plans, but a project tolerance breach goes above the board.
whyNot.1: True that the executive is accountable, but this does not give the board authority beyond project tolerance.
whyNot.2: The project manager prepares exception plans; the business layer decides on project-level exceptions.

reteach.title: The witness who tells the truth about the wrong day
reteach.question: A witness says, truthfully, that the suspect was in London on Monday. The crime was on Tuesday. Is that useful evidence?

blocks.h: True, but about the wrong thing
blocks.body: A true-but-irrelevant option is that witness. Every word is accurate, but it does not speak to the question being asked. In the exam, ask what the question needs explained: who should decide, whether the action was within tolerance, whether a report was needed. Then reject any statement, however true, that answers a different question.

blocks.text: The trap option often repeats words from the stem, such as 'highlight report' or 'tolerance'. Shared words are not the same as an explanation.

explain.body: An option can be wrong because its verdict is wrong, because its reason is false, or because its reason is true but does not explain the situation. The third kind is the hardest to reject.

test.q: A Skyline question asks whether the project manager was right to escalate a delay. Option B says 'Yes, because highlight reports summarize stage status for the board'. The statement is accurate, but escalation was not needed. What kind of option is B?
options: A false statement about highlight reports
A true statement that fails to explain it
The correct answer, as its statement is true
A reason drawn from a different principle
test.why: The statement is accurate in the method but does not explain whether escalating was right, so it is a true-but-irrelevant distractor.

whyNot.0: The description of highlight reports is accurate, so it is not a false statement.
whyNot.2: A true statement is not enough; the reason must explain the situation.
whyNot.3: It is a fact about the progress practice, not a principle's rationale.

test.q: During Skyline's decommissioning stage, disposal costs are forecast to run 2% over plan. The stage cost tolerance is plus or minus 5%. The project manager rearranges two work packages to absorb the cost and notes it in her highlight report. Which reason best explains why this is appropriate?
options: Highlight reports go to the board at intervals it sets
Cost is one of the seven aspects of performance
Within stage tolerance, the PM takes corrective action
Exception reports are an event-driven form of control
test.why: Within stage tolerance, the project manager takes corrective action in controlling a stage without escalating (16.4.6, 11.2.6).

whyNot.0: True, but it explains how reporting works, not why the PM could act herself.
whyNot.1: True, but it does not explain why escalation was not needed.
whyNot.3: True, but no exception report is involved in this action.

test.q: A Stratoshift team manager on Project Skyline forecasts that his work package will exceed its cost tolerance, although the stage as a whole is still within tolerance. What should he do?
options: Raise it with the project manager as an issue
Send an exception report to the project board
Refer it to the society's executive committee
Ask project assurance to approve extra spending
test.why: Team managers escalate a forecast work package breach to the project manager as an issue; the PM handles it in controlling a stage (11.2.1).

whyNot.1: Exception reports are the PM's, and only for forecast breaches of stage or project tolerance.
whyNot.2: The business layer deals with project tolerance breaches.
whyNot.3: Project assurance advises the board; it does not approve spending.

explain.h: Setting tolerances is manage by exception
explain.body: Tolerances set the limits of delegated authority, so setting them applies manage by exception. Manage by stages is about decision points and stage-at-a-time planning.

test.q: At the start of Skyline's wave migration stage, the board sets tolerances for the stage's time, cost and sustainability targets before authorizing the stage plan. Which principle is being applied, and why?
options: 'Manage by exception', because tolerances limit delegated authority
'Manage by exception', because the board reviews each stage at its end
'Manage by stages', because tolerances are agreed for each stage
'Manage by stages', because the PM receives authority stage by stage
test.why: Setting tolerances establishes the limits of delegated authority, which is manage by exception (2.5).

whyNot.1: Right principle, wrong reason: stage-end reviews belong to manage by stages.
whyNot.2: Tolerances are set per stage, but setting them is manage by exception.
whyNot.3: True of manage by stages, but it does not explain setting tolerances.
